1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/ether/etherpad
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: etherpad/etherpad:3.3.3
7	  port: 9001
8	  vm: m1.small
9	  flavor_id: "2"
10	  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0348
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: etherpad
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ ON THE SHIPPED SETTINGS, EVERY PAD IS WORLD READABLE AND WORLD WRITABLE BY URL. This is the single most important line in this file and it is not a bug, it is what Etherpad is. requireAuthentication and requireAuthorization both default to false ([REDACTED:value]:489,494), and webaccess.ts:146-150 then grants the create level to EVERY anonymous request. In practice: anyone who loads your hostname gets the landing page, types any name and has a pad; anyone who guesses or is told a pad name can read it and edit it live; pad names are not secrets and there is no per-pad password. Deployed as-is on a public redu hostname that is an open pad server on infrastructure billed to the user's card, and the first anyone knows is the disk filling. Running it open is a perfectly reasonable DECISION and plenty of people want exactly that. It must be the user's decision, made out loud, and not a default that arrived by accident. This recipe closes it."
18	  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, UNLESS YOU CREATE THEM AT DEPLOY TIME, AND THERE IS NO SIGNUP AT ALL. Etherpad has no registration page, no first-user-is-owner rule and no user directory. The only accounts that can ever exist are the two defined in settings from environment variables: admin, with is_admin true, from ADMIN_PASSWORD, and an ordinary user from USER_PASSWORD ([REDACTED:value]:680-692). Leave ADMIN_PASSWORD unset and the admin password resolves to null and every login is refused, so /admin cannot be entered by anyone, including you. That means there is NO ownership race to lose here: the window is closed by construction, and the job is simply to generate the two passwords before first boot and hand them to the user. ⚠️ Do not be misled by the stale comment at Settings.ts:987-997 claiming that a null default becomes the literal string 'null'. It does not: coerceValue at :1010-1021 has a case for it and returns real null. Read the switch, not the comment."
19	  - "AUTHENTICATED IN ETHERPAD MEANS A SHARED PASSWORD, AND THE USER NEEDS TO KNOW THAT BEFORE THEY CHOOSE. With REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION=true the whole site sits behind HTTP basic auth against those two accounts (webaccess.ts:198-214, which also delays a failed attempt by a second to slow brute forcing). There is no per-person login in core Etherpad, so a team shares one editor password. Each participant still picks their own display name and colour inside a pad, so collaboration works normally; what you do not get is per-user accounts or an audit trail. If the user needs real accounts, that is an authentication plugin and a separate conversation, not a setting. Say this plainly rather than letting them discover that authenticated means one password for everyone."
20	  - "⛔⛔ DB_TYPE DEFAULTS TO dirty, WHICH IS A JSON FILE INSIDE THE CONTAINER, AND IT COMES UP PERFECTLY HEALTHY. [REDACTED:value]:358-366 reads \"dbType\": \"${DB_TYPE:dirty}\" with the file at var/dirty.db, and upstream's own template says in as many words that dirty must not be used for anything but testing or development. Forget DB_TYPE and you get a green health check, a working editor, and every pad, every revision, every author and the rotating cookie signing secrets living in one append-only file that dies with the container on the next redeploy. Set DB_TYPE=postgres. PROVE IT AFTER BOOT IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, because an absence alone proves nothing: run `sudo docker exec <container> printenv DB_TYPE DB_HOST DB_NAME` and confirm postgres and the private database VM (the positive half, which is also what tells you your exec command worked at all), THEN `sudo docker exec <container> ls -la /opt/etherpad-lite/var` and confirm there is NO dirty.db. If the first command errors, the second one's empty output means nothing. The VM runs docker, not podman."
21	  - "ETHERPAD DOES NOT READ DATABASE_URL, SO MAP THE PARTS BY HAND. It wants DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USER and DB_PASS as separate variables ([REDACTED:value]:360-364). deploy_compose with database managed appends PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD and DATABASE_URL to the project .env and never edits your compose, so the compose must interpolate them itself: DB_HOST from ${PGHOST}, DB_PORT from ${PGPORT}, DB_NAME from ${PGDATABASE}, DB_USER from ${PGUSER}, DB_PASS from ${PGPASSWORD}. ⚠️ One consequence of having no URL option: an app that assembles a connection from parts does not survive upgrade_to_ha unchanged, because an HA Postgres publishes pgbouncer on a different port and the old one stops listening. If the user ever upgrades the database to HA, Etherpad has to be redeployed with the new host and port. Say so before they do it, not after."
22	  - "LEAVE DB_CHARSET UNSET FOR POSTGRES. Upstream's compose defaults DB_CHARSET to utf8mb4 while DB_TYPE is postgres in the same block, and utf8mb4 is a MySQL charset name. [REDACTED:value]:365 resolves the setting to undefined when the variable is absent, which is what you want on the postgres driver. This is reasoning from the two files rather than a measured failure, so if you keep it and it works, write that back."
23	  - "⛔ TRUST_PROXY MUST BE true ON REDU, AND UPSTREAM DEFAULTS IT false FOR A REASON THAT DOES NOT APPLY HERE. [REDACTED:value]:505 defaults trustProxy to false, and .env.default explains the tradeoff: on a directly exposed instance false is correct so clients cannot spoof their address, but behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy it must be true. redu ALWAYS terminates TLS at its own proxy and speaks plain HTTP to your container, so this instance is behind one by definition. Leave it false and two things go quietly wrong: Etherpad decides the session cookie is not on a secure connection and omits the Secure flag, and every request looks like it came from the proxy, so client-IP logging is useless and rate limiting is keyed on one address, which means one abusive client rate-limits everybody. Set TRUST_PROXY=true."
24	  - "⛔ THE ADMIN PAGE CAN INSTALL PLUGINS, WHICH IS ARBITRARY CODE EXECUTION ON THE VM. Upstream's own .env.default says exactly that, in the comment above the admin password variable. So ADMIN_PASSWORD is not a formality: it is the key to a shell on the machine. Generate a long random alphanumeric value, hand it to the user once, and never write it into this file or into a compose that gets committed."
25	  - "THERE IS NO ENVIRONMENT SECRET TO PRESERVE HERE, WHICH IS UNIQUE IN THIS LIBRARY, AND IT PUTS EVEN MORE WEIGHT ON THE DATABASE. Every other entry has a variable that silently destroys sessions or encrypted data when it changes. Etherpad v3 does not: the cookie signing secrets are generated and ROTATED automatically and stored IN THE DATABASE under an expressSessionSecrets key prefix (SecretRotator.ts:8,114,176-192, wired in hooks/express.ts:186-198), and Settings.ts:1334-1347 only writes the legacy SESSIONKEY.txt when rotation is turned off, calling the file deprecated. Two consequences worth stating: sessions survive a redeploy as long as the managed database does, and getting the database wiring wrong loses the signing secrets along with the pads. Do not go hunting for a secret variable to set; there is not one."
26	  - "⛔ DELETE THE postgres SERVICE FROM UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE. It ships a postgres:15-alpine with credentials taken from .env.default, so leaving it in while also asking redu for a managed database means paying for two, with the app talking to one. Remove the service and its depends_on entry, then point DB_HOST at the managed database. Also do not carry over the credentials in .env.default: they are published in the repo, which makes them nobody's secret."
27	  - "KEEP BOTH VOLUMES, AND KEEP THEM NAMED. Mount etherpad-var on /opt/etherpad-lite/var and etherpad-plugins on /opt/etherpad-lite/src/plugin_packages. With Postgres wired, var no longer holds your pads, but it is where the dirty fallback would land and where local files go; the plugins volume is what stops any plugin you install through the admin page from vanishing on the next redeploy. Make them NAMED volumes rather than bind mounts from the project directory: the container runs as uid 5001 (Dockerfile ARG EP_UID=5001, USER etherpad) and upstream's compose sets user 5001:0 for exactly this reason, so a root-owned bind mount from your upload is not writable by the process."
28	  - "⛔ ANY SETTING YOU CHANGE IN THE ADMIN UI IS LOST ON THE NEXT DEPLOY. settings.json lives in the image's writable layer, so it survives a container restart and is reverted by a recreate or a pull. Upstream's compose carries a commented-out bind mount for ./settings.json and a comment explaining precisely this. On redu every deploy replaces the container, so treat the admin settings page as read-only and configure everything through environment variables, which is what this recipe does. If the user really wants to edit settings through the UI, that is a bind mount they must add and re-upload, and it then becomes the source of truth instead of the environment."
29	  - "SET DEFAULT_PAD_TEXT TO SOMETHING NON-EMPTY. Upstream's compose comments and .env.default both say the variable appears to be mandatory in current versions, and that with it unset or empty the pad is not established. It costs nothing to set and the failure mode is confusing, so set it."
30	  - "PORT 9001, AND THE HEALTH ROUTE IS PRE-SESSION ON PURPOSE. The Dockerfile exposes 9001 and the image's own HEALTHCHECK wgets http://127.0.0.1:9001/health. GET /health is registered before the session middleware (specialpages.ts:52-58) and returns {\"status\":\"pass\",\"releaseId\":\"<version>\"} as application/health+json, so it answers even with authentication required. That makes it the correct gate for any verification script and the correct probe for a health check; do not point either at / , which is 401 once you close the instance."
31	  - "NO API KEY FILE EXISTS BY DEFAULT, WHICH IS ONE LESS THING TO WORRY ABOUT. Older guides tell you to read APIKEY.txt out of the container to use the HTTP API. In v3 that file is only created when authenticationMethod is apikey (APIKeyHandler.ts:24-33), and [REDACTED:value]:275 defaults it to sso. So there is no long-lived API key sitting in your container unless you ask for one, and if you do want the classic API you are opting into that file and must then persist it."
32	  - "⛔ PIN THE IMAGE, AND WATCH THE develop TAG. etherpad/etherpad:3.3.3 was published 2026-07-29, the same day as latest, 3 and 3.3. The registry ALSO carries a develop tag that was updated 2026-08-15, so it is the newest tag by date and any tooling that sorts by date and takes the top one installs the development branch of a live document server. Pin the exact version."
33	  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. Etherpad talks to the database through ueberdb and sets up its own storage on first connect, so there is no migration step in the repo to run and nothing to schedule. It needs ordinary table-creation rights inside its own database and creates no extensions, so do NOT pass db_superuser and do not worry about redu's one-database-per-managed-Postgres limit: Etherpad uses exactly one."
34	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. Grepped the README and the entire doc tree for a stated RAM or system requirement and got zero hits, with no NODE_OPTIONS or max-old-space setting in the Dockerfile or the compose either. m1.small (1 vCPU / 2 GB) is reasoning from 'one Node process serving a small app with a managed database beside it', and it fits the no-card free trial. The reason the first measurement genuinely matters here: the image runs TypeScript through tsx at RUNTIME (CMD ... node --require tsx/cjs node/server.ts) rather than a prebuilt bundle, and real-time editing keeps every open pad in memory, so a busy instance may want m1.medium. 42	# Self-host Etherpad on redu
43	
44	Real-time collaborative documents on a machine you own: open a URL, share it, and everyone types in
45	the same document at once. One container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL.
46	
47	About GBP 0.035/hour, roughly GBP 25 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.
48	
49	## The decision to make before you deploy
50	
51	Etherpad is, by design, an **open pad server**. On its shipped settings anybody who loads your
52	hostname can create a pad, and anybody who knows or guesses a pad name can read it and edit it. Pad
53	names are not secrets and there is no per-pad password.
54	
55	That is a completely reasonable thing to run, and it is what most public Etherpads are. It is not
56	something to end up with by accident on a hostname billed to your card. So this recipe deploys the
57	**closed** shape by default: the whole site sits behind a password, with exactly two accounts
58	created from environment variables before the first boot.
59	
60	**What "closed" means here, in plain words:** Etherpad has no user directory, so authentication is
61	one shared password for editors and one for the administrator. Everyone still picks their own name
62	and colour inside a pad, so collaboration works normally; what you do not get is per-person
63	accounts. If you want the open shape instead, it is one variable, and this file says which.
64	
65	## What this deploys
66	
67	- **Etherpad** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.small VM, port 9001.
68	- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so pads, revisions and authors survive every
69	  redeploy.
70	- Volumes for local files and for any plugin you install.
71	- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
72	
73	## Deploy
74	
75	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
76	directory containing this file:
77	
78	    Read redu.md and deploy Etherpad on redu.
79	
80	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
81	
82	## The compose
83	
84	Upstream's compose is a good file, but it brings its own Postgres and it defaults `TRUST_PROXY`
85	to false, which is wrong behind redu's TLS-terminating proxy. This is that file with the database
86	removed and the proxy setting corrected:
87	
88	```yaml
89	services:
90	  etherpad:
91	    image: etherpad/etherpad:3.3.3
92	    user: "5001:0"
93	    restart: unless-stopped
94	    environment:
95	      NODE_ENV: "production"
96	      TRUST_PROXY: "true"
97	      DB_TYPE: "postgres"
98	      DB_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
99	      DB_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
100	      DB_NAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
101	      DB_USER: "${PGUSER}"
102	      DB_PASS: "[REDACTED:value]}"
103	      REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION: "true"
104	      REQUIRE_AUTHORIZATION: "false"
105	      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
106	      USER_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
107	      DEFAULT_PAD_TEXT: "Welcome to your pad."
108	    volumes:
109	      - etherpad-var:/opt/etherpad-lite/var
110	      - etherpad-plugins:/opt/etherpad-lite/src/plugin_packages
111	    ports:
112	      - "9001:9001"
113	volumes:
114	  etherpad-var:
115	  etherpad-plugins:
116	```

118	The `PG*` values are injected by redu. The two Etherpad passwords are yours to generate. Set
119	`REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION` to `"false"` only if you have decided you want a public pad server.
120	
121	## The three that actually break it
122	
123	**The database.** `DB_TYPE` defaults to `dirty`, an append-only JSON file inside the container.
124	It comes up perfectly healthy and takes every pad, every revision and the session signing secrets
125	with it on the next redeploy. Upstream's own settings file says not to use it outside development.
126	
127	**The proxy setting.** `TRUST_PROXY` defaults to false, which is right for a directly exposed
128	server and wrong here. Left false, the session cookie loses its Secure flag and every request looks
129	like it came from redu's proxy, so rate limiting punishes everyone for one abuser.
130	
131	**The open default.** Nothing warns you that pads are world-writable. Decide, then set
132	`REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION` on purpose.
133	
134	## Proving the instance is not an open pad server
135	
136	Run this once the deploy reports ready, and before you hand the URL to anyone. It gates every
137	assertion on proof that Etherpad is what is answering, then tests behaviour rather than settings.
138	
139	```bash
140	#!/usr/bin/env bash
141	# Prove this Etherpad refuses anonymous visitors.
142	#   ./verify-closed.sh etherpad-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
143	# Exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN to the internet, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
144	#
145	# Run this ONLY if you deployed the closed shape. If you deliberately chose an open pad server,
146	# a "FAIL" below is your own decision working, and this script is not the right check.
147	set -eu
148	HOST="${1:?usage: verify-closed.sh <host>}"
149	TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
150	
151	inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }
152	
153	# 1. GATE AND POSITIVE CONTROL. /health is registered BEFORE the session middleware, so it answers
154	#    200 even when everything else is behind a password. Its releaseId also proves it is Etherpad
155	#    on this hostname and tells you the version. Without this gate, redu's 502-while-starting page
156	#    would sail through both assertions below, because an error page is not a pad either.
157	code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
158	if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
159	  inconclusive "/health answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
160	fi
161	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
162	  inconclusive "/health answered HTTP $code, not 200."
163	fi
164	grep -q '"status":"pass"' "$TMP/health" || inconclusive "/health returned 200 without a passing status, so this is not Etherpad's health route."
165	grep -q 'releaseId' "$TMP/health"       || inconclusive "/health returned 200 without a releaseId, so this is not Etherpad's health route."
166	echo "OK: Etherpad is serving. Version line: $(cat "$TMP/health")"
167	
168	# 2. ASSERTION ONE: an anonymous request for a pad must be refused.
169	#    The pad name is random so that a 200, if it happens, does not collide with anything real.
170	pad="probe$(date +%s)$RANDOM"
171	code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/p/$pad")
172	case "$code" in
173	  401)
174	    echo "OK: an anonymous pad request was refused."
175	    ;;
176	  200)
177	    echo "FAIL: THIS IS AN OPEN PAD SERVER. An anonymous request for a pad that has never existed" >&2
178	    echo "returned 200, so anyone who finds this hostname can create pads, and read and edit any" >&2
179	    echo "pad whose name they can guess, on a VM you are paying for. If that was NOT the intent," >&2
180	    echo "redeploy with REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION=true." >&2
181	    exit 1
182	    ;;
183	  30*)
184	    inconclusive "a pad request answered HTTP $code, a redirect this script does not follow on purpose. Look at where it points before trusting anything."
185	    ;;
186	  *)
187	    inconclusive "a pad request answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
188	    ;;
189	esac
190	
191	# 3. ASSERTION TWO: /admin must not be enterable anonymously. A 404 here would mean the route
192	#    moved, which proves nothing at all, so it is treated as inconclusive rather than as a pass.
193	code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/admin")
194	case "$code" in
195	  401)
196	    echo "OK: /admin requires authentication."
197	    exit 0
198	    ;;
199	  200)
200	    echo "FAIL: /admin answered 200 to an anonymous request. The admin page can install plugins," >&2
201	    echo "which is arbitrary code execution on the VM. Do not leave this instance running." >&2
202	    exit 1
203	    ;;
204	  404)
205	    inconclusive "/admin answered 404, so the route moved and this probe proved nothing.
206	  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of a 404: a route that exists but rejects the
207	  method answers 405, one that does not exist answers 404."
208	    ;;
209	  *)
210	    inconclusive "/admin answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
211	    ;;
212	esac
213	```

## The three that actually break it

**The database.** `DB_TYPE` defaults to `dirty`, an append-only JSON file inside the container.
It comes up perfectly healthy and takes every pad, every revision and the session signing secrets
with it on the next redeploy. Upstream's own settings file says not to use it outside development.

**The proxy setting.** `TRUST_PROXY` defaults to false, which is right for a directly exposed
server and wrong here. Left false, the session cookie loses its Secure flag and every request looks
like it came from redu's proxy, so rate limiting punishes everyone for one abuser.

**The open default.** Nothing warns you that pads are world-writable. Decide, then set
`REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION` on purpose.

## Proving the instance is not an open pad server

Run this once the deploy reports ready, and before you hand the URL to anyone. It gates every
assertion on proof that Etherpad is what is answering, then tests behaviour rather than settings.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Etherpad refuses anonymous visitors.
#   ./verify-closed.sh etherpad-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN to the internet, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
#
# Run this ONLY if you deployed the closed shape. If you deliberately chose an open pad server,
# a "FAIL" below is your own decision working, and this script is not the right check.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-closed.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. GATE AND POSITIVE CONTROL. /health is registered BEFORE the session middleware, so it answers
#    200 even when everything else is behind a password. Its releaseId also proves it is Etherpad
#    on this hostname and tells you the version. Without this gate, redu's 502-while-starting page
#    would sail through both assertions below, because an error page is not a pad either.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/health answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/health answered HTTP $code, not 200."
fi
grep -q '"status":"pass"' "$TMP/health" || inconclusive "/health returned 200 without a passing status, so this is not Etherpad's health route."
grep -q 'releaseId' "$TMP/health"       || inconclusive "/health returned 200 without a releaseId, so this is not Etherpad's health route."
echo "OK: Etherpad is serving. Version line: $(cat "$TMP/health")"

# 2. ASSERTION ONE: an anonymous request for a pad must be refused.
#    The pad name is random so that a 200, if it happens, does not collide with anything real.
pad="probe$(date +%s)$RANDOM"
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/p/$pad")
case "$code" in
  401)
    echo "OK: an anonymous pad request was refused."
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: THIS IS AN OPEN PAD SERVER. An anonymous request for a pad that has never existed" >&2
    echo "returned 200, so anyone who finds this hostname can create pads, and read and edit any" >&2
    echo "pad whose name they can guess, on a VM you are paying for. If that was NOT the intent," >&2
    echo "redeploy with REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION=true." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  30*)
    inconclusive "a pad request answered HTTP $code, a redirect this script does not follow on purpose. Look at where it points before trusting anything."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "a pad request answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac

# 3. ASSERTION TWO: /admin must not be enterable anonymously. A 404 here would mean the route
#    moved, which proves nothing at all, so it is treated as inconclusive rather than as a pass.
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/admin")
case "$code" in
  401)
    echo "OK: /admin requires authentication."
    exit 0
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: /admin answered 200 to an anonymous request. The admin page can install plugins," >&2
    echo "which is arbitrary code execution on the VM. Do not leave this instance running." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  404)
    inconclusive "/admin answered 404, so the route moved and this probe proved nothing.
  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of a 404: a route that exists but rejects the
  method answers 405, one that does not exist answers 404."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "/admin answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac
```

# Self-host Etherpad on redu

Real-time collaborative documents on a machine you own: open a URL, share it, and everyone types in
the same document at once. One container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL.

About GBP 0.035/hour, roughly GBP 25 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## The decision to make before you deploy

Etherpad is, by design, an **open pad server**. On its shipped settings anybody who loads your
hostname can create a pad, and anybody who knows or guesses a pad name can read it and edit it. Pad
names are not secrets and there is no per-pad password.

That is a completely reasonable thing to run, and it is what most public Etherpads are. It is not
something to end up with by accident on a hostname billed to your card. So this recipe deploys the
**closed** shape by default: the whole site sits behind a password, with exactly two accounts
created from environment variables before the first boot.

**What "closed" means here, in plain words:** Etherpad has no user directory, so authentication is
one shared password for editors and one for the administrator. Everyone still picks their own name
and colour inside a pad, so collaboration works normally; what you do not get is per-person
accounts. If you want the open shape instead, it is one variable, and this file says which.

## What this deploys

- **Etherpad** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.small VM, port 9001.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so pads, revisions and authors survive every
  redeploy.
- Volumes for local files and for any plugin you install.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Etherpad on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's compose is a good file, but it brings its own Postgres and it defaults `TRUST_PROXY`
to false, which is wrong behind redu's TLS-terminating proxy. This is that file with the database
removed and the proxy setting corrected:

```yaml
services:
  etherpad:
    image: etherpad/etherpad:3.3.3
    user: "5001:0"
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: "production"
      TRUST_PROXY: "true"
      DB_TYPE: "postgres"
      DB_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      DB_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      DB_NAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
      DB_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      DB_PASS: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION: "true"
      REQUIRE_AUTHORIZATION: "false"
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      USER_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DEFAULT_PAD_TEXT: "Welcome to your pad."
    volumes:
      - etherpad-var:/opt/etherpad-lite/var
      - etherpad-plugins:/opt/etherpad-lite/src/plugin_packages
    ports:
      - "9001:9001"
volumes:
  etherpad-var:
  etherpad-plugins:
```

The `PG*` values are injected by redu. The two Etherpad passwords are yours to generate. Set
`REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION` to `"false"` only if you have decided you want a public pad server.

## The three that actually break it

**The database.** `DB_TYPE` defaults to `dirty`, an append-only JSON file inside the container.
It comes up perfectly healthy and takes every pad, every revision and the session signing secrets
with it on the next redeploy. Upstream's own settings file says not to use it outside development.

**The proxy setting.** `TRUST_PROXY` defaults to false, which is right for a directly exposed
server and wrong here. Left false, the session cookie loses its Secure flag and every request looks
like it came from redu's proxy, so rate limiting punishes everyone for one abuser.

**The open default.** Nothing warns you that pads are world-writable. Decide, then set
`REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION` on purpose.

## Proving the instance is not an open pad server

Run this once the deploy reports ready, and before you hand the URL to anyone. It gates every
assertion on proof that Etherpad is what is answering, then tests behaviour rather than settings.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Etherpad refuses anonymous visitors.
#   ./verify-closed.sh etherpad-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN to the internet, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
#
# Run this ONLY if you deployed the closed shape. If you deliberately chose an open pad server,
# a "FAIL" below is your own decision working, and this script is not the right check.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-closed.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. GATE AND POSITIVE CONTROL. /health is registered BEFORE the session middleware, so it answers
#    200 even when everything else is behind a password. Its releaseId also proves it is Etherpad
#    on this hostname and tells you the version. Without this gate, redu's 502-while-starting page
#    would sail through both assertions below, because an error page is not a pad either.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/health answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/health answered HTTP $code, not 200."
fi
grep -q '"status":"pass"' "$TMP/health" || inconclusive "/health returned 200 without a passing status, so this is not Etherpad's health route."
grep -q 'releaseId' "$TMP/health"       || inconclusive "/health returned 200 without a releaseId, so this is not Etherpad's health route."
echo "OK: Etherpad is serving. Version line: $(cat "$TMP/health")"

# 2. ASSERTION ONE: an anonymous request for a pad must be refused.
#    The pad name is random so that a 200, if it happens, does not collide with anything real.
pad="probe$(date +%s)$RANDOM"
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/p/$pad")
case "$code" in
  401)
    echo "OK: an anonymous pad request was refused."
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: THIS IS AN OPEN PAD SERVER. An anonymous request for a pad that has never existed" >&2
    echo "returned 200, so anyone who finds this hostname can create pads, and read and edit any" >&2
    echo "pad whose name they can guess, on a VM you are paying for. If that was NOT the intent," >&2
    echo "redeploy with REQUIRE_AUTHENTICATION=true." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  30*)
    inconclusive "a pad request answered HTTP $code, a redirect this script does not follow on purpose. Look at where it points before trusting anything."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "a pad request answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac

# 3. ASSERTION TWO: /admin must not be enterable anonymously. A 404 here would mean the route
#    moved, which proves nothing at all, so it is treated as inconclusive rather than as a pass.
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/admin")
case "$code" in
  401)
    echo "OK: /admin requires authentication."
    exit 0
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: /admin answered 200 to an anonymous request. The admin page can install plugins," >&2
    echo "which is arbitrary code execution on the VM. Do not leave this instance running." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  404)
    inconclusive "/admin answered 404, so the route moved and this probe proved nothing.
  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of a 404: a route that exists but rejects the
  method answers 405, one that does not exist answers 404."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "/admin answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac
```
